title: WHY “DO NOT FEAR MAN” IS HARDER THAN IT SOUNDS
paragraphs:
WHY “DO NOT FEAR MAN” IS HARDER THAN IT SOUNDS
You may never deny Jesus with your mouth. But every time you edit your obedience because you are afraid of someone’s reaction, you discover why Scripture calls the fear of man a trap.
There is a version of you that loves Jesus boldly when nobody is threatening anything.
When the worship music is playing.
When you are surrounded by believers.
When the verse you post gets hearts instead of angry comments.

When obedience does not cost a friendship, disturb a relationship, threaten your reputation, make the room uncomfortable, or force you to choose between being accepted by people and being faithful to Christ.
It is easy to say, “I don’t fear anyone but God.”
Until obedience has a face.
Until the person whose approval you desperately want looks disappointed in you.
Until your family thinks you have become “too serious” about Jesus.
Until your friends begin treating your convictions like an inconvenience.
Until speaking truth could cost you an opportunity.
Until refusing compromise makes you the difficult person in the room.
Until somebody you love says, “If you really cared about me, you wouldn’t believe that.”
Until following Jesus means someone may no longer understand you.
Then suddenly three simple words become painfully expensive:
Do not fear.
And this is where Scripture becomes frighteningly personal.
Proverbs 29:25 says:
“חֶרְדַּת אָדָם יִתֵּן מוֹקֵשׁ וּבוֹטֵחַ בַּיהוָה יְשֻׂגָּב׃”
Ḥerdat ’adam yitten moqesh, u-voteaḥ ba-YHWH yesuggav.

The Hebrew is vivid. חֶרְדַּת אָדָם (ḥerdat adam) speaks of the fear or anxiety of man, and מוֹקֵשׁ (moqesh) is a snare—a trap, a lure, something that catches its victim. The second half turns in the opposite direction: the one trusting in YHWH “will be set on high,” carrying the picture of being placed securely beyond the reach of what threatened to capture him.
Read that again.
The Bible does not merely say the fear of man is unpleasant.
It calls it a snare.
A trap.
And traps rarely announce themselves.
A trap does not stand in the forest screaming, “I am here to destroy you.”
It disguises itself.
So does the fear of man.
Sometimes it calls itself politeness.
Sometimes wisdom.
Sometimes keeping the peace.
Sometimes protecting your reputation.
Sometimes avoiding drama.
Sometimes being “open-minded.”
Sometimes not wanting to offend anybody.

And certainly, Christians are not commanded to become rude, combative, arrogant, reckless, or needlessly offensive. Jesus calls His people to love. Scripture calls us to gentleness. Christian courage is not permission to become cruel.
But there is a difference between gentleness and surrender.
There is a difference between being gracious and being ashamed.
There is a difference between choosing the right moment to speak and spending your entire life waiting for a moment when obedience will cost nothing.
That moment may never come.
Maybe that is why this subject hurts.
Because some of us are not being persecuted into silence.
We are being liked into silence.
We have become so accustomed to approval that disapproval feels like persecution.
One unfollow.
One mocking comment.
One uncomfortable dinner.
One disappointed relative.
One colleague raising an eyebrow.
One friend calling you judgmental.
One person asking, “You actually believe that?”
And suddenly we discover how much power another human being's opinion has been holding over us.
Jesus spoke about fear with words far stronger than most inspirational Christian posts would dare to use.
In Matthew 10:28, the Greek text reads:
“καὶ μὴ φοβεῖσθε ἀπὸ τῶν ἀποκτεννόντων τὸ σῶμα…”
Kai mē phobeisthe apo tōn apoktennontōn to sōma…
“Do not fear those who kill the body…”

Jesus continues by contrasting those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul with the One whose authority extends beyond physical death. The verb φοβεῖσθε (phobeisthe) comes from the language of fear. Jesus is deliberately rearranging the disciples’ hierarchy of fear. Human beings may possess frightening earthly power, but they do not possess ultimate authority.
Notice what Jesus does not say.
He does not tell His disciples that people cannot hurt them.
They can.
That is precisely why His command is so staggering.

Jesus was sending disciples into a world where confessing Him could produce real consequences. Matthew 10 is not motivational advice for becoming more confident around difficult personalities. Christ is preparing His followers for hostility because of their allegiance to Him.
Christian courage, therefore, is not believing, “Nothing bad will happen to me.”
Christian courage says:
“Even if obedience costs me something, Jesus is still Lord.”
That changes everything.
Because perhaps you have misunderstood courage.
Courage is not the absence of trembling.
Sometimes courage is trembling while obeying anyway.
Peter knows something about that.
Hours before the crucifixion, Peter sounded fearless.
Even if everybody else abandoned Jesus, Peter insisted that he would remain.
Then came the courtyard.
The questions.
The accusations.
The pressure.
“You also were with Jesus.”
Suddenly the man who had spoken so confidently discovered something terrifying about himself.
There are things we believe about our courage before the test that the test itself exposes.
Peter denied knowing Jesus.
Not once.
Three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
And Luke records one of the most devastating moments in the Gospel narrative: Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Peter remembered.
And Peter went outside and wept bitterly.
Imagine those tears.
Not merely tears because he had been caught.
Tears because he finally saw himself.
“I said I would die for Him.
I could not even admit that I knew Him.”
Maybe you have never stood in Peter’s courtyard.
But perhaps you have lived your own version of it.
You laughed at something you knew dishonored Christ because you wanted to belong.
You stayed silent when someone asked what you really believed.
You changed your convictions depending on who entered the room.
You removed the Christian post because you worried what people would think.
You compromised because losing that relationship frightened you more than grieving God.
You knew what Scripture said, but you desperately wanted somebody else to approve of you.
You prayed afterward.
You felt sick afterward.
You wondered:
“How could I love Jesus and still be this afraid?”
Peter could answer you.
Because fear of man does not always mean you do not love Jesus.
Sometimes it reveals that there are places inside you where the approval of people is still competing with obedience to Jesus.
And Jesus loves us too much to leave those places hidden.
There is another passage that cuts even deeper.
Paul asks in Galatians 1:10:
“Ἄρτι γὰρ ἀνθρώπους πείθω ἢ τὸν θεόν; ἢ ζητῶ ἀνθρώποις ἀρέσκειν;”
In context, Paul asks whether he is seeking human approval or God's, and whether he is trying to please people. Then comes the devastating conclusion:
“εἰ ἔτι ἀνθρώποις ἤρεσκον, Χριστοῦ δοῦλος οὐκ ἂν ἤμην.”
“If I were still trying to please people, I would not be a servant of Christ.”
Paul is not condemning ordinary kindness.
He is not saying Christians should deliberately make everyone angry.
He is exposing a deeper allegiance.
Who gets the final vote over your obedience?
That is the question.
Because there is a kind of people-pleasing that looks compassionate while quietly enthroning human approval.
And if you need everybody to approve of your obedience before you obey God, they have become more than people whose opinions you value.
They have become people whose permission you require.
That is the snare.
You begin checking faces before checking Scripture.
You measure truth by applause.
You calculate obedience by consequences.
You become one person around believers and another around unbelievers.
You tell yourself that you are protecting relationships when, deep inside, you know you are protecting yourself.
And perhaps the most terrifying part is that you can do this while still appearing deeply religious.
You can sing loudly and fear man.
You can quote Scripture and fear man.
You can preach and fear man.
You can run a Christian page and fear man.
You can have thousands of Christian followers and secretly become addicted to their approval.
You can even tell people not to fear man while refreshing the screen to see whether they approved of the way you said it.
That is how deep the trap goes.
Fear of man is not only a problem “out there.”
It can stand behind a pulpit.
It can hold a microphone.
It can carry a Bible.
It can write this article.
Which means nobody reading this gets to point outward first.
Neither do I.
The Gospel forces us inward before it sends us outward.
“Lord… where am I still afraid of people?”
That question requires courage.
Maybe you fear your parents.
Your spouse.
Your children.
Your employer.
Your pastor.
Your congregation.
Your customers.
Your followers.
Your old friends.
Your new friends.
Maybe there is one person whose disappointment can rearrange your entire emotional world.
You know the person.
You can almost see the face right now.
And if following Jesus brought you into conflict with that person's expectations, you are not completely sure which voice would win.
Do not rush past that.
That may be exactly where Jesus wants to meet you.
Because freedom from the fear of man does not begin with pretending people cannot hurt you.
It begins when Christ becomes more precious than the approval you are terrified of losing.
And this is where the story turns.
Because Peter's courtyard was not the end of Peter.
Thank God.
The man who denied Jesus was not discarded by Jesus.
After the resurrection, Christ came for him.
Jesus restored Peter.
He did not pretend Peter's denial had never happened.
Grace is not amnesia.
Jesus confronted the place of failure and restored the man who had failed.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”
Again.
“Do you love Me?”

The threefold questioning in John 21 has long been noticed beside Peter's threefold denial. Whatever conclusions we draw about every detail of that correspondence, the narrative itself unmistakably shows the risen Christ restoring Peter and recommissioning him to care for His sheep.
The coward in the courtyard did not write the final chapter.
Jesus did.
And there it is.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By redeeming the sinner caught inside it.
Peter's story is not, “A coward finally became impressive enough for God.”
Peter's story is grace.
The cross stands between Peter's shame and Peter's future.
And it stands between yours.
The Gospel is not that courageous people save themselves by becoming fearless.
The Gospel is that sinners—including fearful, compromised, approval-addicted sinners—are reconciled to God through Jesus Christ.
Christ lived in perfect obedience where we have compromised.
Christ remained faithful where we have been ashamed.
Christ went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He died.
He rose.
And those who turn from sin and trust in Him are not merely given a better motivational strategy.
They are given Christ.
Forgiveness.
Grace.
A new allegiance.
A new identity.
A new Lord.
This is why repentance matters.
Repentance is not saying, “I need to become more confident.”
It is saying:

“Jesus, forgive me. I have sometimes wanted their approval more than Yours. I have obeyed my fear. I have protected my image. I have hidden when I should have stood. I have made people too large in my heart and treated You as though You were small. Have mercy on me.”
And He is merciful.
The answer to the fear of man is not self-worship disguised as confidence.
It is not, “Stop caring what everybody thinks because you are amazing.”
That is simply replacing one idol with another.
Biblical freedom comes when God becomes weightier in your heart than human applause.
People can misunderstand you.
Christ knows you.
People can reject you.
Christ remains Lord.
People can mock you.
Christ is not dethroned.
People can unfollow you.
Christ has not moved.
People can remove your seat from their table.
They cannot erase your name from the hands of the Savior who purchased His people with His blood.
And perhaps this is the sentence somebody needs tonight:
You do not have to hate people to stop worshiping their approval.
Love them.
Serve them.
Listen to them.
Honor them where honor is due.
Apologize when you are wrong.
Be gentle.
Be teachable.
Do not confuse stubbornness with holiness.
Do not call every criticism persecution.
Sometimes the person correcting you is right.
Sometimes your behavior—not your Christianity—is what offended them.
Humility must remain beside courage.
But when Scripture is clear, Christ is Lord.
When obedience becomes costly, Christ is Lord.
When your reputation trembles, Christ is Lord.
When your voice trembles, Christ is Lord.
When you lose applause, Christ is Lord.
When following Him makes you misunderstood, Christ is Lord.
And when you fail again?
Run toward Christ, not away from Him.
Peter wept.
Peter was restored.
Peter was changed.
The same disciple once intimidated by questions in a courtyard later stood publicly identifying himself with the crucified and risen Jesus.
That transformation should give frightened believers hope.
Not confidence in themselves.
Confidence in the grace of God.
Maybe you are reading this because you have spent years editing yourself to remain acceptable.
Maybe everybody knows the version of you that causes the least trouble.
Your family gets one version.
Church gets another.
Work gets another.
Social media gets another.
And somewhere underneath all those carefully managed versions is a tired soul whispering:
“I don't even know who I am anymore.”
Come back to Jesus.
You were never meant to carry the impossible burden of being approved by everyone.
You cannot.
Even Jesus was rejected.
So why have we made universal approval the evidence that we are doing Christianity correctly?
The goal is not to become hated.
The goal is faithfulness.
The goal is not controversy.
The goal is Christ.
The goal is not winning arguments.
The goal is obedience flowing from love for the One who first loved us.
And sometimes that obedience will be welcomed.
Sometimes mocked.
Sometimes misunderstood.
Sometimes costly.
But the fear of man is still a snare.
And trust in the Lord is still freedom.
So here is the question I want following you after this article closes:
Whose reaction are you currently allowing to negotiate your obedience to Jesus?
Do not answer quickly.
Name the face.
Name the fear.
Name what you think you could lose.
Then put it before Christ.
Maybe your prayer tonight needs only a few words:
“Jesus, I am afraid.
But I want You more.”
That is not weakness.
That can become the beginning of courage.
And if this exposed something hidden in you, do not hide behind a polished Christian answer.
Pray.
We need Christian spaces where people can admit that following Jesus is sometimes frightening without being treated as spiritual failures.
Supporting Gospel work matters.
But hear this carefully: you cannot purchase God's favor.
Sharing a post does not earn salvation.
No product can purchase grace.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
We support Gospel ministry not to buy God's approval, but because grace has already taught us that the Gospel is worth carrying to others.
If this ministry feeds you spiritually, stay close.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend who walked away from church.
Invite the believer who is exhausted.
Invite the person who is becoming lukewarm.
Invite the person who does not believe yet.
Because somewhere tonight, someone is deciding whether being accepted by people is worth becoming silent about Jesus.
Maybe that person is reading these words.
Maybe that person is you.
Remember Peter.
The courtyard was real.
The denial was real.
The tears were real.
But so was the empty tomb.
So was restoration.
So was grace.
Your worst moment of cowardice does not have to become the final sentence of your story.
Repent.
Come back.
Receive mercy.
Stand again.
And the next time fear whispers, “What will they think of you?”
Remember the better question:
“What has Jesus done for me?”
He was mocked.
Rejected.
Wounded.
Crucified.
Buried.
And He rose.
Your Savior did not remain in the grave.
So do not build your prison from other people's opinions.
The snare is real.
But Christ is greater.
And perhaps the freedom you have been begging God to give you begins the moment you stop asking everyone else for permission to belong completely to Jesus.
The rooster may remind you where you failed—but the empty tomb reminds you Who gets to write what happens next.
